hook.title: Today’s value = today’s reward + tomorrow’s best
hook.text: You don't need to plan the whole trip to know a town's value: it equals **what you get right now** plus **the (discounted) value of the best place you can reach next**. Value looks one step ahead and trusts that the future's value is already right. Walk that idea backwards from the destination (value 0 at the goal, 1 one step before it, $\gamma$ before that…) and you can fill in the whole map. That one-step bookkeeping is the **Bellman equation**.
hook.recall: Remember the one-step rule: $Q^*(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma V^*(s')$ (deterministic) and $V^*(s)=\max_aQ^*(s,a)$. Work backwards from the goal.

explore.intro: Sutton’s A/B gridworld from the slides: from A all actions give +10 and jump to A′; from B +5 to B′; leaving the grid costs −1. $\gamma=0.9$.
tasks: Press *+50 sweeps* and compare with the slide’s $v_*$ grid. Is $v_*(A)\approx24.4$?
Click cell A and read off the Bellman backup. Why does A beat every neighbour?

items: Following the loop back to A takes four more steps of zero reward: $v_*(A')=\gamma^4v_*(A)$

questions.prompt: Chain to a goal with +1 on the final step, $\gamma=0.9$: $V^*(\text{goal})=0$, $V^*(\text{middle right})=1$. What is $V^*(\text{middle})=0+\gamma V^*(\text{middle right})$?

options: There can be multiple optimal policies
All optimal policies share the same $V^*$ and $Q^*$
Different optimal policies have different optimal value functions
questions.explanation: They share $V^*(s)$ and $Q^*(s,a)$ for all $s$ and $(s,a)$.

questions.prompt: *“Even in a deterministic environment, $Q^*(s,a)=\mathbb E_{s'}[\dots]$ requires averaging over many next states.”* What’s wrong?
options: If $s'$ is determined by $s$ and $a$, no expectation is needed: $Q^*(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma V^*(s')$
The expectation must be over actions
There is no Bellman equation in deterministic worlds
